prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Sniper Lee Boyd Malvo said in a letter to CNN that he is still "grappling with shame, guilt, remorse and my own healing if that will ever be possible." And a social worker who has worked extensively with him said he draws self-portraits that often show him with a tear running down his cheek. A self-portrait drawn by sniper Lee Boyd Malvo. Many of his drawings show him with a tear running down his cheek. Malvo, 22, spends 23 hours a day inside his cell at Virginia's toughest prison, a maximum-security compound called Red Onion, not far from the Kentucky border. He's serving a life sentence. According to social worker Carmeta Albarus-Lindo, Malvo is a changed person since he and John Allen Muhammad terrorized the Washington area five years ago this month in attacks that left 10 dead over a 23-day period. "The most I can do is to continue to be there, because that is his greatest fear -- that, you know, another parental figure would abandon him because that was what he'd been exposed to all his life," said Albarus-Lindo, who has spent hundreds of hours with Malvo since his arrest and conviction.  Read the letter » . She said one of those "parental" figures was Muhammad, who met Malvo in the Caribbean nearly two years before the deadly shooting spree began in 2002. Muhammad became the teenager's surrogate father, convincing him that violence was the only way to correct perceived injustices to African-Americans, Albarus-Lindo said. He ordered Malvo to go to bed each night and to memorize passages from "The Art of War," an ancient Chinese text on battlefield strategy. According to Albarus-Lindo, Malvo was "brainwashed" into aiding Muhammad in the murders. However, prosecutors have said Malvo, even at 17, knew what he was doing. "I thought he was coldblooded," said Paul Ebert, commonwealth attorney for Prince William County, Virginia, of the first time he met Malvo. "He was a person who had chosen a life of crime." And when a Virginia jury spared Malvo's life, some investigators said they were horrified. "That was the hardest day of my career," said April Carroll of the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco. "I felt that day we had failed when Malvo was not sentenced to death." Some of the victims' families said they are content that Malvo did not receive the death penalty. Vicki Buchanan Snyder, whose brother James "Sonny" Buchanan was shot in the back while mowing a patch of lawn at a Maryland auto dealership, said she was "satisfied" with the jury's verdict. As for Malvo, Albarus-Lindo said he will "never forgive himself for what has happened." When she first began seeing him, he still called Muhammad "Dad." It took months, she said, before he stopped. In the interim, Albarus-Lindo said, he took college correspondence courses and began to draw. Muhammad is at a Virginia prison called Sussex One. In a DVD made last year inside prison and obtained exclusively by CNN, he said he is "still fighting" on death row. He wants to "correct," he said, some "inaccurate statements" made by the news media about his relationship with Malvo. He wasn't specific about what he meant.  Watch Muhammad on death row » . Muhammad's ex-wife, Mildred, said she believed that she was the real target of the snipers from the beginning. She and her children live in suburban Washington, and she runs a Web site called Afterthetrauma.org, devoted to the victims of domestic abuse. Mildred Muhammad said she feels her ex-husband wanted to kill her as revenge because she was able to gain custody of their three children. As for his relationship with Malvo, she said she too is convinced that John Allen Muhammad brainwashed the younger man. "That boy was a victim before he even knew it," she said. "His life was over when he said, 'Hi.' " E-mail to a friend .

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Sniper Lee Boyd Malvo said in a letter to CNN that he is still “grappling with shame, guilt, remorse and my own healing, if that will ever be possible.”

A social worker who has worked extensively with Malvo said his self-portraits often depict him with a tear running down his cheek.

* A self-portrait drawn by sniper Lee Boyd Malvo. Many of his drawings show him with a tear running down his cheek.

Malvo, 22, is serving a life sentence at Red Onion, Virginia’s toughest prison—a maximum-security compound near the Kentucky border—where he spends 23 hours a day in his cell.

According to social worker Carmeta Albarus-Lindo, Malvo has changed since he and John Allen Muhammad terrorized the Washington area five years ago this month in a 23-day series of attacks that left 10 people dead.

“The most I can do is to continue to be there, because that is his greatest fear—that, you know, another parental figure would abandon him, because that was what he’d been exposed to all his life,” said Albarus-Lindo, who has spent hundreds of hours with Malvo since his arrest and conviction.

*Read the letter »*

Albarus-Lindo said one of those “parental” figures was Muhammad, who met Malvo in the Caribbean nearly two years before the deadly shooting spree began in 2002.

Muhammad became the teenager’s surrogate father and convinced him that violence was the only way to correct perceived injustices against African-Americans, Albarus-Lindo said. He ordered Malvo to go to bed each night and memorize passages from “The Art of War,” an ancient Chinese text on battlefield strategy.

According to Albarus-Lindo, Malvo was “brainwashed” into helping Muhammad commit the murders. Prosecutors, however, have said that Malvo—though only 17 at the time—knew what he was doing.

“I thought he was coldblooded,” Paul Ebert, commonwealth attorney for Prince William County, Virginia, said of his first meeting with Malvo. “He was a person who had chosen a life of crime.”

When a Virginia jury spared Malvo’s life, some investigators said they were horrified.

“That was the hardest day of my career,” said April Carroll of the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco. “I felt that day we had failed when Malvo was not sentenced to death.”

Some victims’ families said they were content that Malvo did not receive the death penalty. Vicki Buchanan Snyder, whose brother, James “Sonny” Buchanan, was shot in the back while mowing a patch of lawn at a Maryland auto dealership, said she was “satisfied” with the jury’s verdict.

As for Malvo, Albarus-Lindo said he will “never forgive himself for what has happened.”

When she first began meeting with him, Malvo still called Muhammad “Dad.” It took months, she said, before he stopped. In the meantime, Albarus-Lindo said, he took college correspondence courses and began drawing.

Muhammad is incarcerated at Sussex One, a Virginia prison. In a DVD recorded inside the prison last year and obtained exclusively by CNN, he said he is “still fighting” on death row. He said he wants to “correct” some “inaccurate statements” made by the news media about his relationship with Malvo, though he did not specify what he meant.

*Watch Muhammad on death row »*

Muhammad’s ex-wife, Mildred, said she believes she was the snipers’ real target from the beginning. She and her children live in suburban Washington, and she runs a website, Afterthetrauma.org, devoted to victims of domestic abuse.

Mildred Muhammad said she believes her ex-husband wanted to kill her in retaliation for her gaining custody of their three children. Regarding his relationship with Malvo, she said she, too, is convinced that John Allen Muhammad brainwashed the younger man.

“That boy was a victim before he even knew it,” she said. “His life was over when he said, ‘Hi.’”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — In a letter sent to CNN, convicted sniper Lee Boyd Malvo wrote that he continues to struggle with shame, guilt and regret, as well as with whether he can ever heal. Carmeta Albarus-Lindo, a social worker who has spent extensive time with him, said many of Malvo’s self-portraits depict a tear running down his face.

Malvo, 22, is serving a life sentence at Red Onion, Virginia’s most secure maximum-security prison near the Kentucky border. He remains confined to his cell for 23 hours each day.

Albarus-Lindo said Malvo has changed since he and John Allen Muhammad carried out a series of attacks that terrorized the Washington region five years ago this month. Ten people were killed during the 23-day shooting spree.

Having spent hundreds of hours with Malvo since his arrest and conviction, Albarus-Lindo said the most important thing she can do is remain present in his life. According to her, his deepest fear is being deserted by another person he views as a parent because abandonment had been a recurring experience throughout his life.

One such parental figure was Muhammad, who met Malvo in the Caribbean almost two years before the fatal shootings began in 2002. Albarus-Lindo said Muhammad became a substitute father to the teenager and persuaded him that violence was the only means of addressing what they regarded as injustices against African-Americans.

Muhammad instructed Malvo when to go to sleep each night and required him to memorize sections of *The Art of War*, the ancient Chinese work on military strategy. Albarus-Lindo believes Muhammad brainwashed Malvo into helping commit the murders.

Prosecutors, however, argued that Malvo understood his actions even though he was only 17. Paul Ebert, the commonwealth’s attorney for Prince William County, Virginia, said his initial impression was that Malvo was coldhearted and had deliberately embraced a criminal life.

Some investigators reacted with horror when a Virginia jury declined to sentence Malvo to death. April Carroll of the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco called it the most difficult day of her career, saying she felt the authorities had failed when Malvo was spared execution.

Some relatives of the victims, however, were comfortable with the decision. Vicki Buchanan Snyder said she was satisfied with the verdict. Her brother, James “Sonny” Buchanan, was shot in the back while mowing a section of grass at a Maryland automobile dealership.

Albarus-Lindo said Malvo will never be able to forgive himself for what occurred. When she began meeting with him, he still referred to Muhammad as “Dad,” and it took several months before he stopped doing so. During that period, Malvo enrolled in college correspondence classes and started drawing.

Muhammad is imprisoned at Sussex One in Virginia. In a DVD recorded inside the prison last year and obtained exclusively by CNN, he said he was continuing his fight while on death row. He also said he wanted to correct what he described as inaccurate media reports about his relationship with Malvo, although he did not identify the specific claims he disputed.

Muhammad’s former wife, Mildred, said she has always believed she was the snipers’ true intended target. She lives with her children in suburban Washington and operates Afterthetrauma.org, a website dedicated to survivors of domestic abuse.

Mildred Muhammad believes her former husband sought to kill her in retaliation for her success in obtaining custody of their three children. She also said she is convinced he brainwashed Malvo, describing the younger man as a victim from the moment they met and saying his life was effectively over as soon as he greeted Muhammad.

CNN’s examination of convicted sniper Lee Boyd Malvo focuses on his life in prison and on the remorse he has expressed for his role in the 2002 Washington-area attacks. Through a letter written by Malvo, a series of self-portraits, and interviews with a social worker and a prosecutor connected to the case, the report presents a man who appears markedly different from the teenager who participated in the shootings.

Malvo was 17 when he and John Allen Muhammad carried out a series of attacks that terrorized the Washington, D.C., region. Ten people were killed and several others wounded as the pair targeted victims seemingly at random. The shootings created widespread fear, leaving residents uncertain about where or when the next attack might occur.

From prison, Malvo has attempted to describe his regret and confront the damage he caused. His writings and artwork suggest intense self-examination, isolation, and sorrow. The self-portraits, in particular, offer a visual record of how he sees himself and his past. Those who have spoken with him say he appears emotionally changed and deeply remorseful, although no expression of regret can undo the suffering inflicted on the victims and their families.

The report also revisits the debate over Malvo’s responsibility. Some people view him as a vulnerable adolescent who was manipulated and psychologically controlled by Muhammad, an older authority figure who became a dominant presence in his life. From that perspective, Malvo was effectively brainwashed and drawn into violence before he had the maturity or independence to resist.

Others, including those involved in prosecuting the case, emphasize that Malvo actively participated in the crimes and must be held accountable for his choices. His youth and Muhammad’s influence may help explain how he became involved, they argue, but they do not erase his responsibility for the deaths.

Malvo’s story therefore remains morally and legally complicated. His apparent transformation in prison raises questions about rehabilitation, juvenile culpability, coercion, and the possibility of genuine remorse. At the same time, the lasting pain of the 2002 attacks ensures that any discussion of his personal growth must remain centered on the lives that were taken and the families and communities that continue to bear the consequences.
